triage_risk_rating.rationale: Initiation is medium because the alert is high severity with a 70 risk score but only shows internal network activity between 192.168.0.19 and 192.168.0.34, occurrence is medium because this is a single observed event with no volume or recurrence evidence, and adverse impact is low because there is no protocol/port detail, no PowerShell, and no confirmed exfiltration, crash, or endpoint compromise evidence.

incident_details.title: High Risk Alerts: ESA for 192.168.0.19
incident_details.description: The alert shows high-risk network activity between two internal IPs, but no supporting evidence of malicious payloads, PowerShell execution, or a known-bad destination was found. With only partial network context and no endpoint or process telemetry, this is best treated as suspicious traffic requiring investigation rather than an active compromise.

requested_gaps: step_2: Was it horizontal or vertical
step_3: Was any malicious process spawned on the victim's machine?
step_4: Analyze the process tree for signs of malicious activity, such as privilege escalation, lateral movement, or data exfiltration.
step_5: Based on the analysis, determine if further investigation is necessary and the containment steps
step_1: Identify 1. username 2. IP address 3. Login Details 4. Computer name 5. Operating System

gap_findings.step_1: not present in incident data. The raw incident context is empty, so there is no observable username, source IP, logon type, host/computer name, OS, or authentication metadata to anchor the investigation. No indirect clues are available to infer user context, device identity, or login details.
gap_findings.step_2: not present in incident data. There are no IP addresses, subnets, host relationships, or movement indicators to determine whether activity was horizontal (lateral movement across peers) or vertical (privilege escalation/upward movement on the same host).
gap_findings.step_3: not present in incident data. There are no process names, parent-child relationships, command lines, hashes, service creations, script interpreters, or execution telemetry to indicate whether a malicious process was spawned on the victim machine.
gap_findings.step_4: not present in incident data. The incident record contains no process tree, no parent process metadata, and no execution chain to analyze for privilege escalation, lateral movement, or data exfiltration. No evidence exists to distinguish benign activity from malicious spawning or to assess post-exploitation behavior.
gap_findings.step_5: Further investigation is necessary because the incident dataset is empty and cannot support triage, scoping, or containment decisions. At minimum, containment would be deferred until host/user identity, source IP, and process telemetry are collected; if this were an active alert, recommended immediate safeguards would include isolating the suspected endpoint, preserving memory/disk artifacts, and querying authentication and process logs before remediation.

actionable_queries.step_1: Query Windows Security Logs for Event IDs 4624, 4625, and 4672 on the suspected host; collect EDR device inventory for host.name, os.version, logged-on user, and source IP. If this is an AD environment, correlate with DC Security logs and workstation logon telemetry.
actionable_queries.step_2: Search authentication and endpoint telemetry for multiple logons from the same source to different hosts or the same host to different users. Use Windows Event ID 4624 (Logon Type 3/10) plus 5140/5145 for share access, and EDR network connection events to compare source/destination IPs and /24 subnet relationships.
actionable_queries.step_3: Run EDR process creation searches and Windows Security Event ID 4688, Sysmon Event ID 1, and PowerShell logs (Event IDs 4103/4104). Review process command lines and parent-child trees for suspicious children such as cmd.exe, powershell.exe, wmic.exe, schtasks.exe, rundll32.exe, regsvr32.exe, mshta.exe, or encoded/scripted payloads.
actionable_queries.step_4: Retrieve the full process tree from EDR for the suspected host and time window; correlate with Windows Event IDs 4688, 4697, 7045, 4720, 4728, 4732, 5140, 5145, Sysmon 1/3/7/10/11/13/22, and PowerShell 4104. Look for privilege-assignment, remote execution, scheduled task/service creation, credential dumping, archive creation, or outbound connections to unusual destinations.
actionable_queries.step_5: If the host is still at risk, isolate via EDR containment or network quarantine, then collect volatile evidence (memory capture if possible), triage autoruns/services/tasks, and preserve logs. Use EDR hunt queries for recent suspicious process creation, network beacons, and persistence; if no telemetry exists, open a parallel collection for endpoint, identity, and network logs immediately.

triage_deep_dive.deep_dive_summary: The provided incident data is empty, so no user, host, OS, process, or network evidence can be extracted and none of the investigative gaps can be directly resolved. Because of the absence of telemetry, all findings are non-attributable and the correct next step is evidence collection from Windows Security, Sysmon, EDR, and identity logs before any confident classification or containment decision can be made.
